title: Tigney Technology Inc. (1997 TCC) Tax Court Decision
subject: Tax Court case examining SR&ED eligibility for wood-pulping technology and the treatment of contract payments.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled against the taxpayer on contract payment deductions (later affirmed in 2000 FCA).
summary: Tigney Technology Inc. v. The Queen (1997, TCC) guides Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED: intercompany management fees recorded as mere book entries are not expenditures made, while pilot plant and U.S. wage costs forming part of a continuous investigation carried on in Canada qualified for investment tax credits at trial—a result the Federal Court of Appeal reversed in 2000 for the expenditures connected with the Kentucky work, rejecting the Tax Court's geographic reasoning.
metaDescription: Learn about the 1997 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Tigney Technology Inc. and its impact on Canadian R&D tax credits.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, entrenched within the legislative architecture of the Income Tax Act (ITA), functions as one of the most structurally complex corporate tax subsidies in the industrialized global economy. The fundamental legislative intent of this program is to mitigate the financial friction associated with technological risk undertaken by Canadian commercial entities. However, this subsidization is strictly conditional. It demands that the physical execution of the scientific method occurs undeniably within the sovereign borders of Canada, and that the financial outlays claimed represent actual, verifiable economic depletion by the taxpayer. The Tax Court of Canada (TCC) decision in Tigney Technology Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, (1997), 97 D.T.C. 414 (T.C.C.), Docket 95-2794(IT)G, serves as a foundational and enduring jurisprudence that meticulously dissects the structural mechanics of intercompany SR&ED agreements, the judicial interpretation of expenditures being "carried on in Canada," and the tax consequences of relying on circular accounting entries rather than economic realities.

Handed down by the Honourable Judge Bell on January 9, 1997, the ruling provides a forensic, courtroom-level examination of a taxpayer's attempt to claim Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) on intercompany management fees alongside outlays associated with pilot plant experiments on tobacco conducted in Edmonton, Alberta, and in Kentucky, U.S.A. The Crown's appeal of this decision was heard by the Federal Court of Appeal in tandem with LGL Ltd. v. R., and in its February 7, 2000 decision in LGL Ltd., the Federal Court of Appeal expressly disagreed with the Tax Court's reasoning in Tigney. In its companion judgment of the same date, Canada v. Tigney Technology Inc. (F.C.A., February 7, 2000, Dockets A-70-97 and A-303-97), the Federal Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal with costs in that Court and in the Tax Court of Canada and set aside the Tax Court's judgment to the extent that it had treated the expenditures connected with the Kentucky work as qualified expenditures for 1993, cementing the rigorous tracing requirements for geographical SR&ED eligibility. This report provides an exhaustive legal, technical, and tax-accounting analysis of the Tigney Technology Inc. ruling, translating the court’s statutory interpretations into applied governance frameworks intended for modern Canadian enterprises and their senior tax advisory counsel.
1.1 The Taxpayer's Claim, Corporate Architecture, and the Operational Mechanics

The Appellant, Tigney Technology Incorporated, operated as a Canadian-resident corporation under the strategic direction of its President and major shareholder, Edward Albert DeLong, who described himself during testimony as self-employed. The overarching corporate mandate of the Appellant was to conduct highly specialized scientific research aimed at separating the various organic components of plant materials, such as trees and straw, while preserving their core structural and chemical integrities for eventual downstream commercialization.

To execute this technical mandate, the Appellant utilized a deliberately compartmentalized corporate structure. It established a wholly owned subsidiary, appropriately named Tigney Research, which was specifically incorporated to isolate the physical research and experimental development activities from the parent company's broader operational or holding functions. Mr. DeLong candidly characterized the subsidiary during his courtroom testimony as an "in-out company," a phrase that would ultimately prove legally fatal to a significant portion of the taxpayer's claim.

The financial and operational architecture binding the parent and the subsidiary was entirely circular and entirely dependent on synthetic bookkeeping mechanisms. Under a Memorandum of Agreement between the two corporations (the Appellant's taxation years ran from June 1 of each year to May 31 of the following year), Tigney Research performed the experimental activities, while Tigney Technology (the parent) assumed the obligation to pay the underlying costs associated with those activities. Upon aggregation of these baseline costs, Tigney Technology would then turn around and charge Tigney Research a rigid 30 percent "management fee," ostensibly intended to compensate the parent for research coordination and management services. Finally, to close the loop, Tigney Research would invoice the total aggregated sum—comprising the base operational costs plus the 30 percent parent-company markup—back to Tigney Technology.

For the 1993 and 1994 taxation years, the Appellant filed the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act to deduct these heavily grossed-up, aggregated amounts and concurrently claim the lucrative Investment Tax Credits under Section 127 of the Act. The specific financial claims placed under dispute by the taxing authority were categorized into two distinct operational tranches, each presenting unique legal vulnerabilities.

The first tranche consisted of the "Pilot Plant Expenditures." These were specific operational amounts of $178,019, $62,411, and $42,223, which the parties agreed were SR&ED and which were designated on a schedule furnished to the Court as "PILOT PLANT IN CANADA," "PILOT PLANT IN U.S.," and "Wages U.S.," respectively. The technical genesis of these expenditures traced back to late 1990, when the Appellant was contacted by Dr. Curt Enzell, an official of Swedish Tobacco. Swedish Tobacco was engaged in a corporate initiative to produce a safer commercial cigarette, a process necessitating the highly complex extraction of specific chemical compounds from raw tobacco biomass. To execute this, Swedish Tobacco shipped dry raw tobacco materials from Sweden to the Appellant. The Appellant initially performed extraction experiments upon this dry, foreign-sourced material in Edmonton, Alberta; however, because extracting the desired pharmaceuticals required fresh tobacco processed within two hours of harvesting, which was not available in Canada, the Appellant's scaled-up portable plant was moved to Kentucky, where 33 or 34 sets of experiments were conducted in November 1992, while all new designs and all analyses of the experimental results were carried out in Edmonton.

The second tranche comprised the "Intercompany Management Fees." These were the specific fiscal manifestations of the 30 percent markup structure detailed in the intercompany Memorandum of Agreement. For the 1993 taxation year, the Appellant's financial statements reflected Management Fee Revenue of $199,289.50. During the trial, counsel for both parties mutually agreed that this specific figure contained a mathematical error, as a factor of 35 percent had been mistakenly utilized instead of the contracted 30 percent; consequently, counsel agreed that the maximum allowable fee would be $175,628. For the 1994 taxation year, an additional management fee amount of $32,733.94 was charged to the subsidiary and subsequently claimed by the parent.
1.2 The Tax Authority's Challenge and the Minister's Reassessment

The Minister of National Revenue, acting as the Respondent in the Tax Court proceedings, issued reassessments against the Appellant that aggressively denied the Investment Tax Credits on multiple, distinct statutory grounds, targeting both the geographic locus of the research and the economic substance of the intercompany fees.

Regarding the first tranche, the pilot plant and U.S. wage expenditures, the Crown's litigation position was narrow. The parties agreed that the amounts of $178,019, $62,411, and $42,223 constituted Scientific Research and Experimental Development as defined in Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. The Crown did not dispute the SR&ED character of these amounts. However, the Minister vigorously disputed the geographic eligibility of the expenditures. The Respondent submitted that the SR&ED represented by each of these amounts was carried on outside Canada—in the case of the $42,223 "Wages U.S.," because the sum was paid to employees while research was being done in the U.S.A. Consequently, the Crown asserted that these expenditures were strictly disqualified from ITC eligibility under the geographic constraints of paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA.

Regarding the second tranche, the intercompany management fees, the issues framed for the Court were whether the amounts of $175,628 for 1993 and $32,733.94 for 1994 were SR&ED, whether they were reasonable in the circumstances, and (for 1993) whether they were allocable between expenditures in Canada and outside Canada. The Crown challenged the fundamental legal and economic reality of the transactions. During a pivotal cross-examination, Crown counsel suggested to Mr. DeLong that the arrangement's only purpose was a gross-up of expenditures to obtain more investment tax credits—which he denied, stating that it had been devised with a major accounting firm—and put to him that there was no gain to Tigney Technology in charging a fee only to have it charged back, to which he replied "I guess not" before stating that he did not understand the question. The Court ultimately characterized these amounts as mere book entries rather than expenditures actually incurred, thereby rendering them wholly ineligible for both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit.
1.3 The Governing Statutory Framework

The ultimate judicial resolution of these highly contested disputes hinged upon a rigorous, textual interpretation of three core components of the Income Tax Act (Canada) and its Income Tax Regulations, read in conjunction with established common law doctrines regarding corporate taxation and economic substance.

Subsection 37(1) of the Act serves as the primary gateway for the deduction of scientific research expenditures. It explicitly provides that where a taxpayer carries on a business in Canada in a taxation year, they may deduct the aggregate of all amounts, each of which is an expenditure of a current nature made by the taxpayer, on scientific research and experimental development "carried on in Canada," provided it is directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and relates to a business of the taxpayer. The critical statutory phrases here are "expenditure made by the taxpayer" and "carried on in Canada," both of which form the battlefield for the Tigney litigation.

Section 127 of the Act provides the secondary, and far more lucrative, mechanism of the Investment Tax Credit. The ITC is calculated as a specified percentage of the "qualified expenditure" made by the taxpayer during the year. A qualified expenditure fundamentally requires an actual economic outlay that satisfies the prerequisites of Section 37. If an amount is deemed not to be an expenditure under Section 37, it automatically fails the qualification test for the ITC under Section 127.

Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, which applied to the 1993 and 1994 taxation years, defines the uncompromising technical parameters of what actually constitutes SR&ED. The regulation mandates that the work must be a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The regulation further delineates this definition into three primary categories—basic research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and experimental development (work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes)—together with supporting work in engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing and psychological research that is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of those categories. Crucially, Regulation 2900 contains strict exclusionary clauses, explicitly barring activities such as market research, sales promotion, quality control, prospecting for minerals, commercial production of a new material, style changes, or routine data collection from being classified as SR&ED.
1.4 The Tax Court's Holding and Its Reversal on Appeal

The Honourable Judge Bell delivered a highly bifurcated ruling that penalized the taxpayer's lack of accounting substance and reliance on intercompany book entries, while simultaneously taking a broad view of a systematic investigation that was carried on predominantly, though not entirely, on Canadian soil.

Regarding the 1993 taxation year, the Court allowed the appeal solely to the limited extent of the pilot plant and U.S. wage expenditures amounting to $178,019, $62,411, and $42,223. Despite the Respondent's submission that this SR&ED was carried on outside Canada, the Court found that the expenditures were made in Canada by a corporation carrying on business in Canada, and that the portion of the research physically conducted in Kentucky—necessitated only because the fresh tobacco required for the experiments was not available in Canada—was an isolated, relatively small and necessary part of a continuous systematic investigation on tobacco carried on in Canada from 1990 until 1993. Therefore, Judge Bell ruled that the relevant sections and regulations of the Act were broad enough to encompass this SR&ED and that all three sums were qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, being expenditures on SR&ED "carried on in Canada" within paragraph 37(1)(a). That part of the judgment did not survive appeal: on February 7, 2000, the Federal Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal and set aside the Tax Court's judgment to the extent that it had treated the expenditures connected with the Kentucky work as qualified expenditures for 1993 (see section 2.2).

However, the Court delivered a total defeat to the taxpayer regarding the intercompany management fees. Judge Bell completely rejected the claims for the grossed-up amounts of $199,289.50 (adjusted to $175,628) for 1993 and $32,733.94 for 1994. The Court concluded definitively that these sums were simply charged by an internal accounting entry to the subsidiary, utilizing the "in-out" mechanism, and were never actually incurred, paid, or economically realized. Relying heavily on established tax precedents, specifically the Canadian case of Ed Sinclair Construction & Supplies Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue and the seminal English House of Lords decision in Gresham Life Society Co. Ltd. v. Bishop, the Court affirmed that a mere bookkeeping entry does not by itself constitute a taxable event or a qualifying expenditure for the purposes of a statutory tax credit; something more, such as an actual receipt, is required.

Because the entirety of the Appellant's claim for the subsequent 1994 taxation year was predicated entirely upon these invalid, circular bookkeeping entries, Judge Bell dismissed the appeal for the 1994 taxation year in its absolute entirety. The Court further ordered that the Appellant was entitled to no further relief and that no costs be awarded; separately, the Court criticized counsel for both parties for failing, before the hearing, to define clearly the issues and amounts involved or to provide the relevant legislation, which required the Court to devote much time and effort to those tasks.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The Tax Court decision in Tigney Technology Inc. functions as a masterclass in statutory interpretation, serving as a cautionary blueprint that details exactly how technical, scientific compliance with Regulation 2900 can be completely and irrevocably nullified by structural failures in corporate governance, contract law, and forensic accounting. The ensuing analysis deconstructs the exact legal, technical, and documentation deficiencies that triggered the Crown's challenge and ultimately led to the disqualification of the management fee portion of the taxpayer's financial claim.
2.1 The Fictitious Expenditure Doctrine: Circular Bookkeeping versus Genuine Economic Outlay

The most devastating legal failure orchestrated by the taxpayer was the structural implementation of the intercompany management fee. Tigney Technology attempted to artificially inflate its eligible SR&ED expenditure base by utilizing its wholly owned subsidiary, Tigney Research, as a mere flow-through entity, attaching an arbitrary 30 percent markup to the baseline costs incurred, and subsequently attempting to claim Investment Tax Credits on the grossly inflated, aggregated amount. This maneuver exposed a fundamental misunderstanding of the legislative mechanics governing tax subsidies.

Under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer may only deduct an amount if it is an "expenditure... made by the taxpayer." The jurisprudence surrounding this phrasing is exceptionally rigid. The statute is designed to subsidize actual financial risk; it does not subsidize hypothetical opportunity costs, theoretical fair market values, or internal profit margins generated between non-arm's length corporate entities. During the trial, the Crown executed a masterful cross-examination that explicitly laid bare the total lack of economic substance underlying the arrangement. The Crown counsel posited to Mr. DeLong: "Sir, there's no gain to Tigney Technology if they're charging say a management fee that's $30,000.00 to Tigney Research and then having to pay it on its way back. I mean, you'll agree to that? I mean, there's no gain to Tigney Technology to do that". Mr. DeLong, who had earlier described the matter as "an accounting question" and the arrangement as "a mechanism for Tigney to obtain the money" required to provide management services, replied "I guess not" before stating that he did not understand the question; the Court ultimately found that no evidence other than the accountants' advice explained the subsidiary's existence and that it did nothing that could not have been done by the Appellant itself.

Judge Bell's rigorous application of the precedents established in Ed Sinclair Construction & Supplies Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue and the historic English House of Lords decision in Gresham Life Society Co. Ltd. v. Bishop (1902) reinforced the doctrine that a mere bookkeeping entry, by itself, does not constitute a taxable event unless there is something more, such as a receipt. The Court quoted Lord Brampton's enduring definition of a receipt from Gresham Life, noting that to constitute a receipt of anything, there must be a person to receive and a person from whom he receives, and something received by the former from the latter—in that case a sum of money—while acknowledging that even a settlement in account may be equivalent to a receipt, and that a mere entry in an account which does not represent such a transaction proves no receipt.

Because the management fee sums of $199,289.50 and $32,733.94 were merely recorded via internal journal entries—without any corresponding transfer of actual funds, liquidation of assets, or the creation of a legally enforceable, arm's-length debt that was subsequently settled in cash—the Court ruled these actions were book entries only, and thus were not expenditures made on SR&ED. Modern implications for Non-Arm's Length (NAL) transactions have only grown more severe since this ruling. While the specific NAL rules within the ITA have evolved significantly since 1997, specifically through the introduction of strict legislative rules restricting SR&ED ITCs to the actual baseline cost incurred by the non-arm's length performer (effectively stripping out any intercompany profit margin by statute), the Tigney ruling established the foundational judicial skepticism toward synthetic intercompany R&D contracts. Any management fee that simply inflates a claim through an "in-out" shell company is viewed by the courts not merely as non-compliant, but as an aggressive, intolerable circumvention of the legislative intent to fund actual scientific risk. Furthermore, modern Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) overhead policies explicitly dictate that arbitrary percentage markups, or methods that arbitrarily connect expenditures with SR&ED work, will not be considered reasonable, rendering such structures entirely unsupportable.
2.2 The Geographic Nexus: "Carried on in Canada" and the Evolution of the Project-as-a-Whole Doctrine

The secondary vulnerability—which the taxpayer overcame at the Tax Court on the specific facts of the 1993 pilot plant and U.S. wage claims, only to lose on appeal, and which led to the Minister's position that the SR&ED was carried on outside Canada—was the physical performance of part of the research in Kentucky, U.S.A., in addition to the use of foreign raw materials and a foreign client relationship.

The Income Tax Act explicitly requires that SR&ED be "carried on in Canada" for an expenditure to be deductible under paragraph 37(1)(a), and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), which governs investment tax credits, is built on the expenditures described in paragraph 37(1)(a). The Minister's stance was that the SR&ED represented by the disputed pilot plant and wage amounts was carried on outside Canada, given that the portable plant had been moved to and operated in Kentucky and that the $42,223 in wages had been paid to employees while research was being done in the U.S.A. This, the Crown argued, placed these expenditures outside the geographic scope of paragraph 37(1)(a).

The taxpayer succeeded at trial in defending these expenditures because it could show, through oral testimony, that the systematic investigation as a whole was centred in Canada. The Court heard, and accepted, evidence that the reactors had been designed in Edmonton with the aid of a Canadian mechanical specialist and the University of Alberta, that the personnel and portable plant were in Kentucky only because the fresh tobacco required for the experiments was not available in Canada, that the November 1992 Kentucky experiments were a small and necessary part of research the Appellant had conducted continuously since 1990, and that all new designs and all analyses of experimental results were conducted in Edmonton.

However, the litigation surrounding this specific geographic point in Tigney Technology Inc. inadvertently birthed a highly controversial, and ultimately doomed, legal doctrine within the Tax Court of Canada, which requires deep analysis by modern tax practitioners. Judge Bell's ruling in Tigney adopted an expressly holistic view of SR&ED, holding that the Kentucky experiments were not a separate and distinct "systematic investigation" but part of continuous research carried on in Canada, so that expenditures for the portion of the work physically performed outside Canada were nonetheless qualified. This reasoning was immediately seized upon by subsequent taxpayers. In the 1998 Tax Court decision Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R., the judge explicitly agreed with Judge Bell's reasoning in Tigney, determining that an SR&ED activity should be looked at as a whole and not artificially subdivided into its constituent, potentially foreign, parts. Similarly, in the initial Tax Court hearing for LGL Ltd. v. R., the taxpayer argued that foreign data collection, when assimilated into a Canadian project, should retain its geographic eligibility; the Tax Court rejected that argument, finding that a substantial part of the project had been performed outside Canada.

This jurisprudential trend was halted by the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in 2000. In LGL Ltd. v. R. (F.C.A., February 7, 2000, Docket A-139-99), whose appeal was heard in tandem with the Crown's appeal in Tigney Technology Inc., the appellate court dismissed LGL's appeal, upheld the Tax Court's per-expenditure approach in that case, and expressly stated that it could not agree with the "project as a whole" geographical reasoning of the Tax Court in Tigney Technology Inc. and Data Kinetics Ltd.; in the companion Tigney judgment, the Court accordingly allowed the Crown's appeal with costs in both courts. Justice McDonald, writing for the FCA, held that this interpretation could not be reconciled with the wording of paragraph 37(1)(a), which focuses on "all amounts each of which is an expenditure" rather than on projects as indivisible wholes. The FCA established the binding precedent that the determination of whether a project is SR&ED under Regulation 2900 is made prior to the determination of whether an SR&ED expenditure was for work carried on inside or outside Canada. Therefore, if a Canadian engineering team spends three weeks conducting experiments in an Edmonton facility, and then spends one week in a Swedish laboratory consulting with foreign peers on the same project, the project cannot be viewed as a whole to grant ITCs on the Swedish labor. The expenditures must be ruthlessly bifurcated: expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada qualify, while the Swedish week can qualify, if at all, only under the limited statutory exception now found in subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA. For expenditures made after February 25, 2008, those provisions treat salary or wages paid to an employee resident in Canada for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, directly undertaken by the taxpayer, related to its business and solely in support of its SR&ED carried on in Canada, as an expenditure on SR&ED carried on in Canada, up to 10 percent of the taxpayer's salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Thus, while Tigney succeeded at the Tax Court in having its Kentucky-related pilot plant and wage expenditures treated as qualified, the FCA's rejection of that reasoning and its reversal of that part of the judgment make the case the genesis of the modern, hyper-strict tracing requirement for Canadian versus foreign SR&ED labor.
2.3 The Evidentiary Burden of Systematic Investigation and the Sass Manufacturing Standard

While the parties agreed that the three disputed pilot plant and wage amounts were SR&ED, Judge Bell quoted in his judgment the evidentiary standard required by Regulation 2900, relying specifically on the precedent set in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. Regulation 2900(1) dictates that SR&ED must be a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis".

The Sass Manufacturing doctrine establishes that the courts require "cogent evidence" of such a systematic investigation. A taxpayer cannot merely point to a successful, or failed, physical prototype on a workbench; they must provide contemporaneous documentation proving the rigorous formulation of a scientific hypothesis, the structured testing of isolated variables, and the continuous documentation of technological uncertainty throughout the iterative development lifecycle. In Tigney, however, the SR&ED character of the disputed amounts was agreed between the parties, and the Court made no finding of any deficiency in the Appellant's scientific documentation; the "PILOT PLANT IN CANADA" label appeared on a schedule of agreed amounts furnished to the Court. The Court's expressed frustration was directed instead at counsel for both parties, who had reached agreements after the pleadings were filed but were unable at the commencement of the hearing to define clearly the issues and amounts, made no useful opening statement, and did not provide the relevant legislation, so that the Court had to devote much time and effort, both at the hearing and in the preparation of the reasons, to tasks that should have been performed by counsel before commencement. Although not the basis of any finding in Tigney, the Sass standard quoted by the Court serves as a warning: failure to maintain contemporaneous, scientifically rigorous documentation mapping directly to the criteria of Regulation 2900 is a structural failure that invites claim denial where SR&ED status is contested, regardless of the brilliance of the underlying engineering.
2.4 Funded Research Exclusions and the Ambiguity of Contractual Intellectual Property

Another critical vulnerability exposed, though not fully litigated to destruction, in the Tigney fact pattern is the dangerous nature of contract-based research and development. The Appellant performed its tobacco experiments after being contacted by Swedish Tobacco and on material sent by it, the cross-examination referred to amounts received by the Appellant for the construction and supply of the refinery, and the relationship with the Swedish company ultimately ended. Under fundamental Canadian SR&ED principles, which have been heavily codified and scrutinized in the decades following the 1990s, if a Canadian taxpayer receives contract payments to perform SR&ED, and the payer retains the exclusive intellectual property rights and bears the ultimate financial risk of failure, the Canadian performer is generally considered to be conducting "funded research." In such scenarios, the performer may have their ITCs severely ground down by the amount of the contract payment, or entirely denied on the basis that the research is not being undertaken "by or on behalf of the taxpayer," but rather on behalf of the client.

Although the Court did not address who bore the financial risk of the scientific endeavor, the intercompany arrangement between Tigney Technology and Tigney Research—described in testimony as "a mechanism for Tigney to obtain the money" required to provide management services—illustrates how loosely justified arrangements invite scrutiny on that issue. If a corporate agreement does not explicitly state, using unambiguous legal terminology, that the Canadian taxpayer retains the right to exploit the Intellectual Property generated, or at a minimum retains the background IP and methodologies, and that the taxpayer bears the technical and financial risk of failure (i.e., they are not guaranteed a fixed fee regardless of outcome), the Canada Revenue Agency will swiftly categorize the work as a standard, commercial provision of services rather than eligible, high-risk SR&ED. The lack of rigorous contractual drafting in Tigney exemplifies the peril of treating legal documentation as an afterthought to the scientific process.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following comprehensive table synthesizes the specific statutory and regulatory mandates of the Income Tax Act, maps them directly against the operational realities and failures present in the Tigney Technology Inc. case, and details the exacting standards of proof applied by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. This matrix serves as an essential diagnostic tool for senior tax advisors evaluating the compliance posture of modern SR&ED claims.

Part of the systematic investigation was physically performed outside Canada, leading the Minister to treat the related expenditures as SR&ED carried on outside Canada.

(heard in tandem), ruled that the "project as a whole" doctrine is invalid for the geographic test; geographical eligibility is assessed strictly on a per-expenditure, per-activity basis after Regulation 2900 qualification.

The taxpayer engaged in complex processes for separating plant materials. The parties agreed the disputed pilot plant and wage amounts were SR&ED; the Court criticized counsel for both parties for failing to define the issues and amounts before the hearing.

The Court made no finding of deficient scientific documentation; the "PILOT PLANT IN CANADA" schedule summarized agreed amounts. The case nonetheless illustrates the value of contemporaneous scientific logs detailing hypotheses, variables, and iterations.

Standard Restated (TCC). Citing Sass Manufacturing, Judge Bell quoted the requirement for "cogent evidence" of the scientific method. The Court awarded no costs to either party, but did not tie that order to the evidence; its criticism concerned counsel's failure to clarify the issues, amounts and legislation.
Corporate Governance / Substance over Form

Tigney Research was described as an "in-out" company set up, on accountants' advice, to keep all research costs in one pot; the parent charged it a 30% management fee, which was then charged back to the parent together with Research's other costs.
The Court found no evidence, other than the accountants' advice, explaining the subsidiary's existence, and found that it did nothing that could not have been done by the Appellant.

Failed (TCC). The Court did not pierce the corporate veil; it examined the substance of the intercompany entries and concluded that the management fees were not expenditures made by the Appellant, because no money for services was actually expended.
CRA Overhead Policy Compliance (Post-Case Implication)
The taxpayer attempted to claim a blanket 30% fee for "research coordination and management services" provided by the parent.
The taxpayer used an arbitrary, fixed percentage to allocate management costs to the SR&ED pool without proving direct, incremental linkage to specific scientific activities.

Not Reached (TCC) / Failed Under Modern Policy. Although reasonableness was among the issues framed, the Court disallowed the fees solely because they were not expenditures made. Modern CRA policy, informed by such cases, dictates that fixed cost contracts and arbitrary percentage allocations fail the incremental test for SR&ED overhead. Only directly attributable, reasonably allocated costs are permissible.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To seamlessly translate the judicial findings, statutory interpretations, and severe legal warnings of Tigney Technology Inc. into highly actionable corporate strategy, the following case studies apply the court’s logic to complex, modern industrial scenarios. These studies demonstrate precisely how a senior Canadian R&D tax credit attorney would aggressively restructure a project's governance framework, technical documentation protocols, and financial tracking systems to bulletproof an SR&ED claim against the exact pitfalls identified by Judge Bell and the subsequent Federal Court of Appeal.
4.1 Case Study 1: The Transnational CleanTech Joint Venture (Overcoming Geographic and Evidentiary Burdens)
Scenario Context:

Aurora Bio-Extraction Inc., a highly capitalized Canadian clean-technology engineering firm headquartered in Calgary, Alberta, has entered into a lucrative joint venture contract with a Swiss pharmaceutical consortium. The objective is to develop a novel, proprietary methodology for extracting highly volatile medicinal compounds from specialized European alpine flora. The Swiss consortium provides the initial biochemical baseline data, full funding for the initiative, and the raw, frozen flora imported directly from Zurich. Aurora will conduct all the physical stress testing, chemical solvent trials, and iterative process redesigns. The engineering team consists of five Canadian chemical engineers based in Calgary, and two Swiss biochemists who direct the overarching project goals via daily video link and physically visit the Calgary laboratory for one week every month.
Identified Legal Vulnerabilities (The Tigney Pitfalls):

Without immediate and severe legal intervention, the Canada Revenue Agency will inevitably audit this project and deny the SR&ED claim in its entirety, deploying arguments similar to the Minister's position in Tigney that SR&ED connected with work performed outside Canada was carried on outside Canada. The CRA will assert that the project is heavily integrated with a foreign entity, the raw materials are exclusively foreign, foreign engineers are actively directing the daily scientific work, and the resulting intellectual property ultimately benefits a Swiss corporation. Furthermore, relying on the Federal Court of Appeal's 2000 ruling that rejected the TCC's generous "project as a whole" interpretation, the CRA will attempt to strip out any hours tangentially related to the Swiss engineers. Finally, if Aurora relies on end-of-year engineering summaries rather than "cogent evidence," they will completely fail the Sass Manufacturing standard quoted by Judge Bell.
Step-by-Step Restructuring and Remediation Plan:

First, the tax counsel must execute strict Contractual Ring-Fencing to address Intellectual Property and Financial Risk. The SR&ED claim must not be disqualified under the "funded research" provisions. The Canadian attorney must renegotiate or explicitly draft the Statement of Work (SOW) with the Swiss consortium prior to the commencement of any scientific activity. The contract must stipulate in unambiguous terms that Aurora Bio-Extraction Inc. is not being paid a guaranteed fixed fee for a guaranteed, commercially viable result. Instead, the contract must explicitly state that Aurora bears the financial risk if the iterative testing requires substantially more labor hours or solvent materials than initially budgeted. Furthermore, to satisfy the requirement that the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED, the contract must grant Aurora the irrevocable right to utilize the underlying testing methodologies (the background IP) developed during the project for other future clients, even if the Swiss firm retains the specific foreground patent on the extracted alpine compound.

Second, the operational team must enforce the Geographic Segregation of Labor, adhering to the post-Tigney FCA mandate. To ensure absolute compliance with ITA paragraph 37(1)(a), the project governance must establish a strict "Canadian SR&ED Polygon." The corporate time-tracking system (such as Jira or SAP) must be reconfigured with highly specific, geofenced task codes that isolate physical work executed in Calgary. The remediation requires that the two Swiss specialists' time is strictly and permanently excluded from the Canadian SR&ED claim pool. Crucially, when the Canadian engineers consult with the Swiss team via video link to discuss project parameters, this specific time must be coded as "General Project Management—Non-SR&ED." Only the precise, tracked hours the Canadian engineers spend physically inside the Calgary laboratory—running the solvent degradation simulations, manipulating the frozen flora, and analyzing the mass spectrometry data—are permitted to be coded to the SR&ED eligible pool. This granular tracing preempts any CRA attempt to disqualify the labor based on foreign contamination.

Third, the engineering department must implement the Sass Manufacturing Evidence Standard. Although the SR&ED character of Tigney's disputed amounts was agreed by the parties, the Court in Tigney quoted the Sass Manufacturing requirement of "cogent evidence" of a systematic investigation, and a summary schedule alone would not meet that standard where SR&ED status is contested. To prevent such an evidentiary collapse, Aurora must implement a Contemporaneous SR&ED Logging Protocol. Before the European flora is subjected to the first solvent test, the Lead Canadian Engineer must draft a formal, one-page "Technological Uncertainty Document" detailing exactly why standard thermodynamic equations and existing biochemical literature cannot predict the flora's cellular breakdown behavior under pressure. During testing, the team must maintain a secure, timestamped digital lab notebook recording every single failed iteration. If a cellular structure fractures improperly at 80°C, the date, time, exact pressure parameters, and resulting negative data must be logged instantly. This protocol provides the unassailable "cogent evidence" of a systematic investigation required by Regulation 2900, proving the work was genuine experimental development rather than routine, ineligible data collection.
4.2 Case Study 2: The Intercompany R&D Cost Center (Eliminating Circular Bookkeeping Fictions)
Scenario Context:

Quantum Aerospace Parent Corp. is a large Canadian holding corporation. It owns 100 percent of Quantum Test Labs Ltd., a subsidiary corporation created solely to act as an isolated cost center to conduct high-risk aerodynamic wind-tunnel testing. During the fiscal year, Quantum Test Labs incurs $2,000,000 in actual, verifiable researcher salaries and specialized lab supplies. At the fiscal year-end, the Chief Financial Officer of the Parent Corp. directs the accounting department to have Quantum Test Labs invoice the parent company for $2,600,000. This figure represents the $2,000,000 actual baseline cost plus a $600,000 (30 percent) arbitrary management and coordination markup. Absolutely no cash changes hands between the bank accounts of the two entities; the entire $2,600,000 transaction is recorded merely as an intercompany payable on the parent's ledger and an intercompany receivable on the subsidiary's ledger. Quantum Aerospace Parent Corp. then attempts to file a Section 37 claim and collect an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit on the full, grossed-up $2,600,000.
Identified Legal Vulnerabilities (The Tigney Pitfalls):

This corporate scenario closely resembles, in structure and intent, the operational architecture deployed in Tigney Technology Inc., where a 30 percent management fee was recorded through intercompany book entries and charged back to the parent. The Canada Revenue Agency will immediately and aggressively disallow the $600,000 markup because it is a non-arm's length profit element that lacks any basis in economic reality. In Tigney, the Court applied the precedents of Ed Sinclair Construction and Gresham Life Society Co. Ltd. to deny only the management fee amounts, which were mere book entries; however, where—as here—the entire $2,600,000 transaction exists only as a journal entry, the same reasoning creates a risk that the CRA will challenge whether any part of the entire $2,600,000 SR&ED claim was an expenditure actually made by the parent. Because the transaction is executed as a mere bookkeeping journal entry with no actual receipt or verifiable outlay of money, the CRA will classify it as a sham transaction or a legally void fiction for tax purposes, resulting in a total loss of the tax credits and potential gross negligence penalties.
Step-by-Step Restructuring and Remediation Plan:

First, the tax advisor must mandate the immediate Eradication of the Artificial Markup. The Canadian tax counsel must forcefully instruct the CFO to completely eliminate the 30 percent management fee from the SR&ED calculation. Under the strict, modern interpretation of the Income Tax Act regarding non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, the eligible expenditure can never exceed the actual baseline cost incurred by the performer. The remediation requires that the intercompany invoice must be adjusted downward to exactly $2,000,000. All SR&ED claims generated within a consolidated or non-arm's length corporate group must be executed on a strict, transparent cost-recovery basis, ensuring zero internal profit is subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer.

Second, the legal team must establish genuine Commercial and Legal Substance through an Agency or Bare Trust structure. The "in-out" mechanism described by Mr. DeLong in the Tigney testimony—although set out in a Memorandum of Agreement—failed because the management fees it generated were book entries only, and such an arrangement is indefensible during an audit. The attorney must draft a highly formalized "Intercompany R&D Cost Sharing and Agency Agreement" before the fiscal year begins. This legally binding contract must explicitly designate Quantum Test Labs Ltd. as a legal agent acting entirely on behalf of Quantum Aerospace Parent Corp. The agreement must state unequivocally that the Parent Corp. directs all research objectives, automatically owns all resulting Intellectual Property immediately upon its creation, and is legally obligated to reimburse the subsidiary for all direct, verified costs incurred during the execution of the mandate.

Third, the finance department must execute Actual Economic Outlays to provide the Gresham Life Cure. To survive an audit based on Judge Bell's rigorous ruling, the parent company must prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that an actual expenditure was made. A journal entry in an intercompany loan account is utterly insufficient. The remediation requires the accounting department to execute a physical wire transfer, or issue a cleared bank draft, from Quantum Aerospace Parent Corp.'s corporate bank account to Quantum Test Labs' operating bank account for the exact, reconciled sum of $2,000,000. This transfer must occur before the end of the taxation year or, at the latest, within 180 days after its end: under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, an expenditure described in paragraph 37(1)(a) that is unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is treated as not incurred in that year and as incurred only when it is paid, and the section 78 unpaid-amount rules can also apply to amounts owed to a non-arm's length party. Separately, the claim itself must be filed on the prescribed form no later than one year after the corporation's filing-due date for the year, the SR&ED reporting deadline. The validated bank statements showing the cash leaving one account and entering the other must be attached directly to the T661 SR&ED schedule as definitive, irrefutable proof of an "expenditure incurred," thereby entirely nullifying any Crown argument of circular bookkeeping or paper fictions.

Fourth, regarding the substantiation of indirect costs, if Quantum Aerospace wishes to claim legitimate overhead expenses (rather than relying on a fictional management fee), it must utilize the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) mechanism currently available in the modern ITA, or it must strictly allocate actual overhead costs (such as facility electricity or specific administrative support salaries) using a highly reasonable, rigorously documented allocation base (e.g., the precise square footage of the wind-tunnel lab, or exact hours worked by support staff). As illustrated by the failure of the 30 percent fee in Tigney—which the Court disallowed because it was a book entry rather than an expenditure made—arbitrary percentage markups applied without a direct, traceable, and incremental linkage to the scientific work are highly vulnerable to denial by the tax authority.
